abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Valemetostat tosylate (valemetostat) is an oral, potent, dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH) 2 and EZH1 under investigation for the treatment of cancer, including non‐Hodgkin's lymphomas and solid tumors. Itraconazole and fluconazole are antifungal medications often used as typical inhibitors of cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A [itraconazole and fluconazole]) and P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp [itraconazole]) in drug–drug interaction studies. Valemetostat is a substrate of CYP3A and P‐gp in vitro. This phase I, open‐label, single‐sequence crossover study (JapicCTI‐183902) assessed the pharmacokinetics (PK) of valemetostat when co‐administered with itraconazole (a strong CYP3A inhibitor and P‐gp inhibitor) or fluconazole (a moderate CYP3A inhibitor) in healthy Japanese male participants 20–45 years of age. Participants were equally allocated to receive two doses of valemetostat 25 mg, once alone and once with either itraconazole or fluconazole (400‐mg induction and 200‐mg once daily maintenance). Valemetostat PK parameters with versus without itraconazole or fluconazole were compared using analysis of variance models. Overall, 32 participants were enrolled. Co‐administration with itraconazole increased valemetostat peak concentration (C max) by 2.9‐fold and area under the plasma concentration–time curve extrapolated to infinity (AUCinf) by 4.2‐fold compared with valemetostat alone. When co‐administered with fluconazole, the C max and AUCinf of valemetostat were each increased by 1.6‐fold. No treatment‐related or grade ≥3 adverse events were reported. Appropriate valemetostat dose reductions are warranted when used concomitantly with strong CYP3A and P‐gp dual inhibitors.

p.bold: WHAT IS THE CURRENT KNOWLEDGE ON THE TOPIC?

boxed-text.p:
Valemetostat is an oral, potent, dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH) 2 and EZH1 recently approved in Japan for treatment of relapsed/refractory adult T‐cell leukemia/lymphoma. Valemetostat is a substrate of cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A) and efflux transporter P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp). The pharmacokinetics (PK) of CYP3A or P‐gp substrate drugs can be impacted by concomitant use of CYP3A or P‐gp modulators. Therefore, drug–drug interaction (DDI) studies are warranted to assess target drug PK when used concomitantly with these agents.
WHAT QUESTION DID THIS STUDY ADDRESS?

This phase I DDI trial assessed the PK of valemetostat when co‐administered with itraconazole, a strong CYP3A and P‐gp inhibitor, or fluconazole, a moderate CYP3A inhibitor, to inform dosing recommendations when used concomitantly with CYP3A or P‐gp inhibitors.
WHAT DOES THIS STUDY ADD TO OUR KNOWLEDGE?

Co‐administration of valemetostat with itraconazole increased mean maximum plasma concentration (C max) by approximately threefold and mean area under the plasma concentration–time curve (AUC) from time‐0 extrapolated to infinity (AUCinf) by approximately fourfold relative to valemetostat alone. Valemetostat and fluconazole co‐administration increased both valemetostat C max and AUCinf by ~1.6‐fold.
HOW MIGHT THIS CHANGE CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY OR TRANSLATIONAL SCIENCE
These findings indicate the need for dose adjustments when valemetostat is used concomitantly with strong CYP3A and P‐gp dual inhibitors.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Valemetostat tosylate (valemetostat; DS‐3201b) is an oral, potent, and selective dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH) 2 and EZH1. 1 , 2 EZH2 and EZH1 are histone methyltransferases that catalyze the attachment of three methyl groups to histone H3, a repressive transcriptional mark that silences genes by compressing chromatin and preventing transcription. 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 EZH2 and EZH1 play key roles in tumor cell growth and survival, and overexpression of EZH mutations has been implicated in the progression of non‐Hodgkin's lymphomas (NHLs), including adult T‐cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL). 3 , 5 , 8 , 9 , 10

Valemetostat is approved in Japan (as EZHARMIA; Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd.) for treatment of patients with relapsed/refractory ATLL at a dose of 200 mg once‐daily (q.d.), 11 and is in clinical development for the treatment of other hematologic malignancies and solid tumors. 1 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 In a multicenter, single‐arm, phase II trial of valemetostat monotherapy in 25 patients with relapsed/refractory ATLL, valemetostat 200 mg/day was associated with an overall response rate of 48.0% (12/25; 90% confidence interval [CI] 30.5% to 65.9%), inducing complete remissions in four patients. 14 The primary treatment‐emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were myelosuppression, alopecia, dysgeusia, decreased appetite, and pyrexia. 14

Patients with hematologic malignancies are at increased risk of infection, including fungal infections. 16 , 17 Treatment and prophylaxis with antifungal medications, including itraconazole and fluconazole, are often warranted in high‐risk patients. 16 Itraconazole and fluconazole are known strong and moderate inhibitors of cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A, respectively, and itraconazole also inhibits P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp). Itraconazole is often used as a strong CYP3A inhibitor in clinical drug–drug interaction (DDI) studies, as recommended by the Innovation and Quality in Pharmaceutical Development Clinical Pharmacology Leadership Group. 18 Valemetostat has been identified in vitro as a substrate of CYP3A and P‐gp (unpublished data). The pharmacokinetic (PK) profiles of other medicinal drugs that are substrates of CYP3A and/or P‐gp are substantially altered when used in combination with CYP3A or P‐gp inhibitors. For example, co‐administration of midazolam with 200 mg itraconazole causes a 10‐ to 15‐fold increase in the area under the plasma concentration–time curve (AUC) of midazolam, and co‐administration with fluconazole (400 mg loading and 200 mg q.d. maintenance) causes a 3.6‐fold increase in the AUC of midazolam. 19 In addition, a 200‐mg dose of itraconazole increased both the AUC and maximum plasma concentration (C max) of fexofenadine (single dose 60 mg), a P‐gp substrate, by twofold when co‐administered. 20 Accordingly, patients receiving valemetostat and CYP3A or P‐gp inhibitors may be at risk for DDIs that could impact valemetostat PK, potentially increasing bioavailability and exposure.

To inform potential valemetostat dose adjustments when used concomitantly with a CYP3A or P‐gp inhibitor, we conducted a phase I DDI study to assess the effects of multiple oral administrations of itraconazole and fluconazole on the PK of valemetostat in healthy Japanese adult males.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This was a phase I, open‐label, single‐sequence crossover study (JapicCTI‐183902) that enrolled healthy Japanese males 20–45 years of age with a body mass index (BMI) of greater than or equal to 18.5 to less than 25.0 at screening. Healthy participants were determined based on their medical history, physical examinations, vital signs, 12‐lead electrocardiograms, and clinical laboratory tests during screening. Exclusion criteria included a history of clinically significant diseases, including cardiovascular, respiratory, blood, hematopoietic, gastrointestinal, or central nervous system disorders, or other disorders that could potentially risk the safety of participants, such as hepatic/renal impairment, thyroid dysfunction, pituitary malfunction, and adrenal insufficiency. Participants were required to have abstained from any medications, including supplements containing St. John's Wort, for 30 days before hospital admission and until the post‐study or follow‐up examination. Additionally, consumption of grapefruit juice was prohibited within 7 days of admission.

The trial was performed at Souseikai Fukuoka Mirai Hospital (Fukuoka, Japan) and conducted in compliance with the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki, the International Council for Harmonization of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use Consolidated Guideline E6 for Good Clinical Practice, and Japanese regulatory requirements. The study protocol was approved by the local institutional review board. All participants provided written informed consent prior to screening.

Eligible participants were assigned to the itraconazole or fluconazole dosing groups (1:1 allocation) and received two single oral doses of valemetostat 25 mg tablets, first alone on day 1 and then concomitantly with either itraconazole on day 11 or fluconazole on day 12 (Figure 1). Itraconazole (Itrizole capsules; Janssen Pharmaceutical KK) was administered orally from day 6 through day 20 at a dose of 400 mg (200 mg twice daily [b.i.d.]) on day 6 and 200 mg q.d. on days 7–20. Fluconazole (Diflucan capsules; Pfizer Japan ) was administered orally q.d. on days 6–18, as 400 mg on day 6 and 200 mg on days 7–18. The 25‐mg valemetostat dose assessed in this trial allowed for an eightfold AUC margin relative to the 200‐mg dose‐level that was shown to be safe and well‐tolerated in the first‐in‐human phase I trial in patients with relapsed/refractory NHL (NCT02732275), 21 and in a separate phase I trial comprising healthy Japanese adults (JapicCTI‐173804). 22

caption.p: Treatment schedules for the itraconazole and fluconazole groups.

sec.p: The study participants were admitted to the hospital from the day before the initial dose of valemetostat until the day after the final administration of the concomitant drug, with a total period of 21 nights and 22 days for the itraconazole group and 19 nights and 20 days for the fluconazole group. During the hospitalization period, the study center provided all meals and beverages to the participants, and consumption of any other food or beverages was strictly prohibited. The meals were served at designated times, and the beverages provided were free of caffeine. Participants were prohibited from smoking or engaging in excessive physical exercise during their hospital stay.

Valemetostat was administered following a 10‐h fast and subjects were to remain fasted for at least 4 h postdose. Itraconazole and fluconazole were administered after breakfast (itraconazole was also taken after dinner on day 6) except on day 11 or day 12 when valemetostat and itraconazole/fluconazole were taken together under fasted conditions. On days without valemetostat administration, meals were provided 30 min prior to administration of itraconazole or fluconazole and finished within 20 min. All study drugs were taken with 240 mL of water and subjects were instructed to remain in a sitting position for at least 4 h postdose. Participants were hospitalized for ~20 days and then followed for an additional 13–15 days for monitoring of potential TEAEs. Use of drugs other than valemetostat, itraconazole, or fluconazole was prohibited from 30 days prior to the first dose until the end of the follow‐up period, unless required for intervention of an adverse event.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic evaluations
sec.p: Blood samples were collected to determine valemetostat, itraconazole, and fluconazole plasma concentrations. The PK profile of valemetostat alone was determined from blood samples collected prior to valemetostat dosing on day 1, and at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h postdose. Next, to assess the impact of itraconazole and fluconazole on valemetostat PK, blood samples were collected prior to valemetostat dosing on day 11 (itraconazole group) or day 12 (fluconazole group), and at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 24, 48, 72, 96, 120, 144, and 168 h postdose, and again at 240 h postdose in the itraconazole group. Prospective blood collections at the greater than or equal to 24 h timepoints were performed prior to itraconazole/fluconazole dosing. Plasma concentrations of itraconazole and fluconazole were assessed on day 6 before their administration alone, and before co‐administration with valemetostat on day 11 for itraconazole or day 12 for fluconazole. Subsequently, measurements were taken prior to itraconazole dosing on day 15 and day 21 (96 and 240 h after co‐administration with valemetostat on day 11), and before fluconazole on day 16 and day 19 (96 and 168 h after co‐administration with valemetostat on day 12).

Pharmacokinetic parameters assessed included C max, time to reach C max (T max), AUC up to the last quantifiable timepoint (AUClast) and extrapolated to infinity (AUCinf), terminal elimination half‐life (t 1/2), oral clearance (CL/F), and apparent volume of distribution (Vz/F). The primary PK end points were C max, AUClast, and AUCinf of valemetostat when administered alone and when co‐administered with itraconazole or fluconazole; T max, elimination rate constant associated with the terminal phase, t 1/2, CL/F, and Vz/F were secondary end points. Plasma concentrations of valemetostat, itraconazole, and fluconazole were measured using a validated liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry method (Data S1). For valemetostat, a 20‐μL aliquot of plasma sample was subjected to protein precipitation with acetonitrile after the addition of deuterium‐labeled valemetostat (valemetostat‐d6) as an internal standard. The resulting supernatants were diluted with 5 mmol/L ammonium formate containing 0.01% formic acid, and then injected on a reversed phase liquid chromatography column. Mass spectrometric detection was performed using an API5000 triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (Sciex), equipped with a Turbo‐IonSpray source. Multiple reaction monitoring in the positive mode was used for detection. The validated concentration range was 1–1000 ng/mL for valemetostat. The lower limit of quantification was 1 ng/mL. The within‐ and inter‐day assay precision (percent coefficient of variation) for quality control samples were in the ranges of 0.6%–5.9% and 1.6%–4.9%, respectively, and the assay accuracy percentages were in the ranges of 90.3%–105.3% and 93.7%–102.0%, respectively.

Pharmacokinetic parameters for valemetostat were calculated via a noncompartmental analysis using Phoenix WinNonlin version 6.3 (Certara). The PK analysis set included participants who received valemetostat alone (day 1) and in combination with itraconazole (day 11) or fluconazole (day 12), with available PK data from both assessments.

sec.title: Safety evaluations
sec.p: Safety was assessed via TEAE reporting and monitoring of clinical laboratory parameters. Participants were evaluated for TEAEs from the first dose through the end of the follow‐up period (approximately days 31–35). TEAEs were defined using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 21.0 and graded for severity was assessed according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.0, Japanese edition by the Japan Clinical Oncology Group.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: No statistical hypotheses were tested to set a sample size in this study. However, the sample size of 16 subjects in each treatment would be sufficient to provide PK parameters to evaluate the magnitude of changes in valemetostat exposures based on previous PK observations. The PK parameters of valemetostat when administered alone versus with concomitant itraconazole or fluconazole was compared using an analysis of variance model, which used a linear mixed effect model with natural logarithms as response variables, treatment period (alone/concomitant) as fixed effects, and participants as a random effect. The natural logarithms were inversely transformed, and the geometric least‐squares (LS) mean ratio of test (valemetostat + itraconazole or valemetostat + fluconazole) versus reference (valemetostat alone) and its two‐sided 90% CI was calculated for relevant parameters. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute).

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Overall, 32 participants were enrolled and assigned to the itraconazole or fluconazole groups (n = 16 each). All 16 participants in the itraconazole group completed the study. In the fluconazole group, 13 participants completed the trial; three participants in this group discontinued due to TEAEs (n = 2; described below) and participant decision (n = 1) after receiving valemetostat alone but before starting fluconazole on day 6.

Baseline characteristics were similar between the itraconazole and fluconazole groups. Mean (standard deviation [SD]) ages in the itraconazole and fluconazole groups were 28.3 (6.15) and 30.6 (5.46) years, respectively; mean BMIs were 21.4 (1.77) and 21.2 (1.63; Table 1).

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic evaluations
sec.p: The PK analysis set comprised all 16 participants in the itraconazole group and the 13 participants in the fluconazole group. Co‐administration of valemetostat with itraconazole or fluconazole increased plasma concentrations of valemetostat. Mean plasma concentration–time profiles for valemetostat administered alone and with itraconazole or fluconazole are presented in Figures 2 and 3, respectively. Following a single administration of valemetostat 25 mg, median (range) T max of valemetostat alone was 3.5 (1.0–5.0) h in the itraconazole group and 3.0 (0.5–6.0) h in the fluconazole group, and when co‐administered with itraconazole and fluconazole was 3.0 (1.0–4.0) and 4.0 (1.0–5.0) h, respectively (Table 2). When co‐administered with itraconazole, mean t 1/2 of valemetostat was prolonged more than twofold, from 17.5 alone to 39.2 h with itraconazole, whereas valemetostat t 1/2 was similar with or without concomitant fluconazole (19.2 and 21.7 h, respectively; Table 2). Descriptive mean values for valemetostat C max, AUClast, and AUCinf were each higher when taken with itraconazole or fluconazole versus valemetostat alone.

sec.p: Statistical comparisons of valemetostat C max, AUClast, and AUCinf when co‐administered with or without itraconazole and fluconazole are presented in Table 3. The geometric LS mean of valemetostat C max when co‐administered with itraconazole was nearly three times higher relative to valemetostat alone (LS mean ratio 2.92), and geometric LS means for AUClast and AUCinf were each more than four times greater with itraconazole + valemetostat (LS mean ratios 4.30 and 4.19, respectively, vs. valemetostat alone). When co‐administered with fluconazole, geometric LS mean ratios for C max, AUClast, and AUCinf were each ~1.6‐fold higher versus valemetostat alone: 1.61, 1.63, and 1.58, respectively. Comparisons of valemetostat C max, AUClast, and AUCinf values for individual participants with and without concomitant itraconazole or fluconazole administration are presented in Figure 4.

sec.p: Prior to co‐administration with valemetostat, the mean [SD] plasma concentrations of fluconazole and itraconazole were 7240 [1130] and 353 [138] ng/mL, respectively. Fluconazole plasma concentration remained stable until 168 h post co‐administration (mean 7770 [1270] ng/mL). Mean itraconazole concentration gradually increased to 447 [156] ng/mL 96 h after co‐administration with valemetostat and 615 (244) ng/mL after 240 h.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: All 32 enrolled participants received at least one dose of valemetostat and were evaluated for safety. As mentioned, 29 (91%) participants received both planned valemetostat doses, once alone (day 1) and once with itraconazole (day 11) or fluconazole (day 12), and the three other participants only received one dose of valemetostat and discontinued before the second dosing period.

The overall TEAE incidence rates were 12.5% (2/16 participants) in the itraconazole group and 50.0% (8/16) in the fluconazole group. All 10 participants who experienced TEAEs had low‐grade upper respiratory tract infections that were likely related to a sudden onset of cold weather and were not suspected to be related to the study drug. These infections were grade 1 in severity for nine participants and grade 2 for one participant, and all events resolved within 1–4 days of onset. Eight events occurred during the valemetostat‐only dosing period and two occurred during the itraconazole or fluconazole (n = 1 each) co‐administration dosing period. One participant in the fluconazole group received acetaminophen as symptomatic treatment on day 4. Two of these events, including the one that required medication, led to study discontinuation during the valemetostat‐only dosing period. No deaths, serious TEAEs, or grade greater than or equal to 3 TEAEs were reported in either group.

Increases in C‐reactive protein were noted in 10 participants and neutrophil/leukocyte count increases were seen in three participants, all of which were attributable to the upper respiratory tract infections. No other clinically significant changes in laboratory parameters, vital signs, and physical examination were observed.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p:
It is important to assess potential clinically relevant DDIs between valemetostat and other drugs, especially those frequently needed by patients with cancer. Co‐administration of valemetostat with itraconazole resulted in approximately three‐ and fourfold increase in valemetostat C
max and AUC, respectively. In addition, co‐administration with itraconazole prolonged valemetostat t 1/2 from 17.5 to 39.2 h, when compared with valemetostat alone.

Valemetostat is a substrate of CYP3A and P‐gp, and itraconazole is a potent inhibitor of both molecules. Therefore, the observed effect of itraconazole on valemetostat C max and AUC was attributable to an increase in the bioavailability and a reduction in the elimination of valemetostat. The magnitude of increase in valemetostat exposure was considerably large, which suggests that appropriate dose modifications are warranted for valemetostat when used concomitantly with strong CYP3A and P‐gp dual inhibitors, like itraconazole.

Co‐administration with fluconazole resulted in a moderate increase in both C max and AUC (~1.6‐fold). The similar t 1/2 of valemetostat with or without fluconazole suggested that the inhibition of CYP3A‐mediated metabolism primarily occurs in the first‐pass metabolism, and the effect of fluconazole on the elimination is less pronounced than with itraconazole. Fluconazole is also known as a strong inhibitor of CYP2C19 and a moderate inhibitor of CYP2C9. However, in the present DDI assessments, the effect of fluconazole is only limited to its CYP3A inhibition, as valemetostat metabolism is not mediated by those CYP isoforms (unpublished data). In a recent phase II trial of valemetostat monotherapy in 25 patients with relapsed/refractory ATLL (NCT04102150), 14 valemetostat 200 mg/day was administered without dose adjustment to 11 patients with concomitant use of fluconazole. Grade greater than or equal to 3 TEAEs reported were comparable in seven of 11 patients (63.6%) versus seven of 12 (58.3%) with and without fluconazole, respectively. Serious TEAEs were higher in the subgroup with fluconazole (45.5%) compared to those without fluconazole (8.3%). However, most serious TEAEs were considered to be due to patients' primary disease, complications, or other concomitant medications, and therefore not related to the increased exposure of valemetostat observed in the fluconazole group. These results suggested that co‐administration of valemetostat with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors does not warrant dose adjustment.

A limitation of this study is the valemetostat dose of 25 mg used for the DDI assessments. Although the safety and tolerability of valemetostat in healthy adults has been explored in single doses of up to 200 mg, 22 the reduced 25‐mg dose used in this study was selected to protect the safety of healthy participants, given the anticipated amplification of valemetostat PK when taken with itraconazole or fluconazole. In healthy subjects, valemetostat PK appears to be dose‐proportional in the range of 25–200 mg; however, the involvement of CYP3A‐mediated metabolism and P‐gp–mediated transport could be different between these doses. In this trial, itraconazole was used as a typical therapeutic agent with strong CYP3A inhibitory activity, and it also inhibits P‐gp. Given the complexity of how drug metabolism and transport affect the absorption and disposition of valemetostat, physiologically‐based PK (PBPK) model analyses were further performed to evaluate the impact of CYP3A and P‐gp inhibition on valemetostat PK. Results from PBPK modeling and simulation confirmed the effects of itraconazole and fluconazole at clinically relevant dose (i.e., 200 mg q.d.). In addition, the effects of a strong CYP3A‐selective inhibitor and a P‐gp–selective inhibitor on valemetostat exposure were explored, the details of which will be presented in a future report.

No increases in the incidences of TEAEs or other safety concerns were identified from the co‐administration of valemetostat with either itraconazole or fluconazole in healthy adults. No adverse events, including the upper respiratory tract infections reported in 10 participants, were suspected to be related to valemetostat. During an infection, the inflammatory response leads to elevated pro‐inflammatory cytokine levels. Cytokines such as interleukin 6 are known to downregulate the expression of CYP3A4, influencing the clearance of drugs that are CYP3A4 substrates. 23 Subject cytokine levels were not assessed during this study, and it remains unclear whether the infections reported in this trial have impacted CYP metabolism and valemetostat PK results.

In this study, co‐administration of valemetostat with itraconazole or fluconazole was well‐tolerated but increased valemetostat exposure. Although the extent of valemetostat's interaction with moderate to strong CYP3A inhibitors and P‐gp inhibitors at a clinically relevant dose of 200 mg may be altered, the study findings are supported by previous data, including valemetostat's observed dose‐proportional PK response ranging from 25 to 200 mg, and safety data from a phase II trial involving patients who received 200 mg of valemetostat concurrently with fluconazole. These data will help to provide dosing instructions for valemetostat and DDI risk management. The safety and tolerability of valemetostat in patients with NHL and other cancers when co‐administered with CYP3A and/or P‐gp inhibitors will further be assessed in future clinical trials and postmarketing evaluations.
